INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
Amici are fifty-six veterans of the United States
Armed Forces whose service spans the Army, Marine
Corps, Navy, and Air Force from the late 1970s to the present.  Their relevant experience includes training with,
carrying, maintaining, and instructing others in the use of
military service rifles.  They submit this brief in their individual capacities to offer a practical military perspective
on the AR-15-style rifles banned in Cook County and Connecticut and to explain the military significance of the capabilities retained by those rifles.  The individual amici
are identified in Appendix A.2
In addition to their military service, some amici are
also current gun owners, and therefore have experience
with both civilian firearm ownership and firearm use in
military service.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
To serve our nation, we were trained on and have experience using the military-designated M16 and M4 rifles.
Petitioners argue that these rifles are fundamentally different from AR-15s, which are semiautomatic assault
weapons.3 Grant Pet. Br. 16.  As veterans, we know that
is not the case.
1 No counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or in part.  No
party or counsel for a party made a monetary contribution intended
to fund its preparation or submission.  No person other than amici or
their counsel made such a contribution.
2 The views expressed herein are solely those of the individual
amici and do not reflect the official policy or position of any service
branch, the U.S. Department of Defense, or the U.S. Government.
Amici join in their individual capacities, and their views do not represent the views of any organization or entity.
3 This brief uses “assault weapons” to refer to the semiautomatic
rifles covered by the challenged laws and at issue here, following the

2
We write to share our perspective on the similarities
between the weapons we used in military service and the
AR-15 rifles covered by the laws at issue in this case. 4
These weapons functionally are equivalent to their military counterparts, like the M4 and M16; while the military
versions may have additional firing modes, members of
our military are trained to use semiautomatic fire in all
but narrow circumstances, and as a result rarely, if ever,
use these additional modes.  Further, these service rifles
share design and operating features identical to the AR-
15.
Having served in the military, we know what makes a
weapon effective in combat.  We agree with U.S. Army
veteran and Fourth Circuit Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson
III, speaking for the Fourth Circuit en banc: “The primary difference between the M16 and AR-15—the M16’s
capacity for automatic fire, burst fire, or both, depending
on the model—pales in significance compared to the
plethora of combat-functional features that makes the two
weapons so similar.”  Bianchi v. Brown, 111 F.4th 438, 456
(4th Cir. 2024) (en banc).  The judgments below should be
affirmed.
terminology in those laws and respondents’ submissions.  See Conn.
Gen. Stat. § 53-202a(1); Cook County, Ill., Code § 54-211.
4 This brief focuses on the AR-15 and functionally equivalent rifles
made by other manufacturers.  For brevity, this brief uses “AR-15”
to refer to all these AR-15-style rifles.

3
ARGUMENT
I. IT IS U.S. MILITARY POLICY TO USE
SEMIAUTOMATIC FIRE EVEN WHEN BURST OR
FULLY AUTOMATIC MODES ARE AVAILABLE,
EXCEPT IN NARROW CIRCUMSTANCES
In delineating the scope of the Second Amendment
right as held by private citizens, this Court has indicated
that those “weapons that are most useful in military service—M-16 rifles and the like—may be banned.”  District
of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570, 627 (2008).  Here, the
United States, as amicus for petitioners, attempts to distinguish AR-15s from those bannable weapons because
they lack “the capacity for fully automatic fire.”  U.S. Amicus Br. 20 (U.S. Sept. 4, 2026).  This distinction ignores
how these weapons actually are used in military service,
including combat situations.  M16 and M4 military rifles
are used almost exclusively in semiautomatic mode, as
service members are trained to do, even when more rapid
firing is available.  Amici’s military experience, and sworn
declarations filed in another case by two experts with decades of military service (one of whom is participating as
amicus here), confirm that riflemen—consistent with
their training—“almost never” use the automatic or burst
capabilities of their standard-issue service rifles.  Report
of Lieutenant Colonel Jason Dempsey, U.S. Army retired
¶ 16 (June 8, 2024), Ex. 1 to Declaration of Jason Dempsey, Barnett v. Raoul, No. 3:23-cv-00209 (S.D. Ill. Sept. 6,
2024), Dkt. No. 222-3 (Dempsey Barnett Report).  As set
out below, such use would more often impair rather than
serve combat objectives.
A. Civilian AR-15s Are Identical to M16s and M4s in
Design and Operation When Fired in Semiautomatic Mode
The civilian AR-15 is operationally identical to the
M16 and the M4 in all respects but one—the military

4
versions can fire in burst or fully automatic mode in addition to semiautomatic mode.  See Dempsey Barnett Report ¶ 15.  In semiautomatic mode, each shot requires a
separate trigger pull.  In burst mode, the rifle will fire
three rounds with each trigger pull.  In fully automatic
mode, it will fire until the trigger is released.  An M4 in
fully automatic mode also will stop firing when it exhausts
the magazine capacity—which in the military is almost always 30 rounds and therefore exhausts quickly in fully automatic mode.
Each variant of the M16 and M4 can toggle between
semiautomatic fire and either burst or automatic fire, depending on the model.  The table below, from the Army’s
active training circular on rifles and carbines, lays out the
firing modes of common military service rifle variants.
U.S. Dep’t of the Army, Training Circular 3-22.9, Rifle
and Carbine  Tbl. 2-1 (May 2016, last updated Nov. 20,
2019) (2016 Manual).  The M4 is a carbine: a shorter,
lighter version of the M16 with a 14.5-inch barrel (versus
20 inches) and a collapsible stock.  Ibid.
The similarities between these military service rifles
and civilian AR-15s have been explored in assault weapons cases in the courts of appeals and district courts—including in decisions upholding the Connecticut and Cook
County laws against Second Amendment challenges.  See,

5
e.g., Grant Pet. App. 47a–48a; Viramontes Pet. App. 14a–
15a, 23a–24a; Barnett v. Raoul, 180 F.4th 1035, 1053–1054
(7th Cir. 2026); Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 454–456; Bevis v.
City of Naperville , 85 F.4th 1175, 1195–1196 (7th Cir.
2023), cert. denied, 144 S. Ct. 2491 (2024); Capen v. Campbell, 708 F. Supp. 3d 65, 85 (D. Mass. 2023), aff’d, 134 F.4th
660 (1st Cir. 2025); Rupp v. Bonta, 723 F. Supp. 3d 837,
852 (C.D. Cal. 2024). Retired Marine Colonel Craig
Tucker and retired Army Lieutenant Colonel Jason
Dempsey each provided a sworn declaration in one of
these cases, and Colonel Tucker provided a declaration in
another, based on their knowledge and experience as military veterans.
Colonel Tucker and Lieutenant Colonel Dempsey are
experienced veterans with extensive knowledge of the
military’s training and use of firearms.  Colonel Tucker
commanded numerous infantry units and battalions during his 25 years of service, including in intense infantry
combat in Iraq.  Report of Colonel (Ret.) Craig Tucker ¶ 1
(June 7, 2024), Ex. 1 to Declaration of Craig Tucker, Barnett v. Raoul, No. 3:23-cv-00209 (S.D. Ill. Sept. 6, 2024),
Dkt. No. 222-2 (Tucker Barnett Report).  After returning
from Iraq, Colonel Tucker trained and certified units for
combat in Iraq and Afghanistan at the Marine Corps National Training Center.  Ibid.  Lieutenant Colonel Dempsey served in the U.S. Army for 22 years after graduating
from the U.S. Military Academy at West Point.  Dempsey
Barnett Report ¶¶ 1, 14.  Over the course of his career, he
was deployed to Afghanistan and Iraq and trained or supervised the training of thousands of infantry riflemen for
combat.  Id. ¶¶ 1, 18.
As the testimony of Colonel Tucker and Lieutenant
Colonel Dempsey describes, when operated in semiautomatic mode, an M16 or an M4 is no different from an AR-
15. See Supplemental Expert Report and Declaration of
Colonel (Ret.) Craig Tucker ¶¶ 1, 13, Rupp v. Bonta, No.

6
8:17-cv-00746 (C.D. Cal. May 26, 2023), Dkt. No. 151-15
(Tucker Rupp Report).  They have “the same rates of fire,
the same maximum effective range, the same maximum
range, [and] use the same magazines designed for combat
and the same ammunition.”  Id. ¶ 13.  Thus, an M4 or M16
rifle in semiautomatic mode fulfills a military purpose that
would be equally well-served by a semiautomatic AR-15
platform rifle.  See Dempsey Barnett Report ¶ 34.
B. The Military Directs the Use of Semiautomatic
Mode for M16s and M4s in Nearly All Instances
Because It Is More Accurate, Efficient, and Reliable than Automatic or Burst Fire in a Combat Setting
“[S]emi-automatic fire is the preferred method of employment” for military service rifles like the M16 and M4.
Tucker Barnett Report ¶ 10.  According to the Army’s
2008 marksmanship manual, “[t]he most important firing
technique during fast-moving, modern combat is rapid
semiautomatic fire.”  U.S. Dep’t of the Army, FM 3-22.9,
Rifle Marksmanship: M16-/M4-Series Weapons  7–8, ¶ 7-
12 (Aug. 12, 2008) (2008 Manual) (emphasis added).  For
this reason, “M16 rifles and M4 carbines should normally
be employed in the semiautomatic fire mode.”  Id. at 7-13.
Amici elaborate below on three reasons why using
semiautomatic fire with a service rifle is preferable to automatic or burst fire in a combat setting.
Accuracy: An M16 or M4 firing in semiautomatic mode
is more accurate than the same weapon firing in automatic
or burst mode.  The 2016 Manual explains why this is so:
“[a]utomatic or burst fires drastically decrease the probability of hit due to the rapid succession of recoil impulses
and the inability of the Soldier to maintain proper sight
alignment and sight picture on the target.”  2016 Manual
at 8-6; see also 2008 Manual at 7-12 (“Automatic or burst
fire is inherently less accurate than semiautomatic fire.”).

7
Lieutenant Colonel Dempsey explained that if a threeround burst is fired, “the first bullet may hit its intended
target, but the recoil of the weapon is likely to send the
next two rounds well above the initial point of aim.”
Dempsey Barnett Report ¶ 19.  And the accuracy problems are “only exacerbated” with fully automatic fire.
Ibid.  Rather than increasing combat effectiveness, an
M16 or M4 set to fully automatic mode is “difficult to control and providing aimed fire of any type is very challenging.”  Tucker Barnett Report ¶ 13.
Lieutenant Colonel Dempsey provided an example of
how this works in a combat situation.  In a basic four-man
infantry unit, the rifleman armed with an M16 or M4 is
tasked with “placing well-aimed fire on the enemy,” which
requires semiautomatic fire.  Dempsey Barnett Report
¶ 21 (quoting U.S. Dep’t of the Army, ATP 3-21.8, Infantry Rifle Platoon and Squad, (Jan. 2024)).  Meanwhile, another team member is responsible for providing “a high
volume of sustained suppressive” fire—the rifleman
armed with an M249 machine gun.  Ibid. (quoting same).
Unlike the M16 and M4, the M249 machine gun “is stabilized” with components that allow for “automatic fire that
is both more rapid and more accurate than can be provided” by burst or automatic fire from a typical service
weapon.  Id. ¶ 23.  Thus, in the instances where the military sees tactical benefit to fully automatic fire, it uses a
weapon specifically designed for this purpose.
Efficiency: Semiautomatic fire allows for ammunition
discipline—the management, tracking, and control of how
many rounds are expended—making it more efficient
than automatic or burst fire.  Automatic fire and burst fire
both use more ammunition than semiautomatic rifle fire
because those modes expend more than one bullet when
the trigger is held.  The 2008 Manual directs that “[a]utomatic or burst fire should be used sparingly” to conserve
ammunition.  2008 Manual at 7-17.  The rare instance in

8
which Colonel Tucker witnessed automatic fire from an
M16 or M4, during the First Battle of Fallujah, resulted
in “a critical ammunition shortage.”  Tucker Barnett Report ¶ 11.  Army materials similarly link effective semiautomatic fire to ammunition conservation.  See 2008 Manual at 7-9, 7-15.
Reliability: An M16 or M4 fired in automatic or burst
mode is more likely to jam or overheat, making it less reliable.  These weapons are “not designed to fire on automatic for extended periods of time” and overheating can
lead to misfires and magazine feed issues.  Tucker Barnett
Report ¶ 13; see also 2016 Manual at 2-13 (describing the
challenge of cooling “[l]ightweight weapons like the M4
and M16”).  Of course, any heating issue or jam resulting
from automatic fire can put a rifleman “at greater risk of
becoming combat ineffective.”  Dempsey Barnett Report
¶ 24.
Amici do not contend that automatic or burst fire has
no application.  The 2008 Manual recognizes that “[i]n
some combat situations, the use of automatic or burst fire
can improve survivability and enhance mission accomplishment.”  2008 Manual at 7-13.  For example, “limited
use of automatic or burst fire” may be required to clear
buildings and ambushes.  Ibid.  However, the manual directs that such fire “should be used sparingly and only to
gain initial fire superiority.”  Id. at 7-17.
C. Consistent with Their Training, Combat Veterans
Used M16s and M4s Almost Exclusively in Semiautomatic Mode and Rarely, if Ever, Used Burst
or Fully Automatic Fire
Military doctrine makes semiautomatic fire the default, see Part I.B, supra, and veterans’ firsthand accounts
confirm that the default holds in training and in combat.
The experience of Lieutenant Colonel Dempsey, who
trained thousands of infantry riflemen over the course of

9
a 22-year Army career, reflects this clear preference for
semiautomatic mode.  He “never once trained or instructed any infantry rifleman to use an M4/M16 service
rifle on the 3-round burst or fully automatic setting.”
Dempsey Barnett Report ¶¶ 14, 16–18.  Instead, he
trained “each and every one of them to fire exclusively on
the semiautomatic setting.”  Id. ¶ 18; see also 2008 Manual
at 7-13.  Nor did Lieutenant Colonel Dempsey ever use
his own service rifle for burst or automatic fire.  Dempsey
Barnett Report ¶ 16.  He testified that this training and
practice reflected an intentional choice to use semiautomatic fire because of the benefits of that firing mode in
combat situations.  Id. ¶¶ 16, 22.
Colonel Tucker’s experience was similar.  Like Lieutenant Colonel Dempsey, he “almost exclusively” emphasized semiautomatic fire in qualification, training, and
combat.  Tucker Barnett Report ¶¶ 10–13 (emphasis omitted).  And he “never once saw any infantry member fire
their rifle on automatic” apart from “very short auto
bursts upon room entry” during the First Battle of Fallujah.  Id. ¶ 11.  Chief Warrant Officer 5 Marine Gunner Jeffrey Eby described his own M4 combat firing as “[a]lways
in semi-auto.”  Deposition of Jeffrey Eby 40:13-15 (July
18, 2024), Barnett v. Raoul, No. 3:23-cv-00209 (S.D. Ill.
Sept. 13, 2024), Dkt. No. 232-3; see also Bianchi, 111 F.4th
at 456 (“decorated former U.S. Navy SEAL” “‘never once
fired full auto in combat’ during a decade of special operations combat deployments, including the 2011 Osama Bin
Laden raid”).
The testimony of these veterans is instructive and accords with amici’s experiences in military service.
 * * *
In sum, although military service rifles like the M16
and M4 are capable of fully automatic or burst fire, the
United States military uses these modes exceedingly

10
rarely.  Instead, these weapons are routinely used and
taught to be used on the semiautomatic setting, such that
they operate just like civilian AR-15s.  The capability for
automatic or burst fire cannot justify prohibition of M16s
or M4s but not AR-15s.
II. THE BANNED AR-15 FEATURES COMBAT-RELATED
DESIGN ELEMENTS
A military rifle like the M16 and M4, fired semiautomatically, is “no different than” the AR-15.  Tucker  Barnett Report ¶ 15; see also Kyleanne Hunter, The Role of
Assault Weapons in Mass Shooting Incidents: State of the
Science 4–5, testimony before the S. Comm. on the Judiciary (July 20, 2022), RAND CT-A2184-1 (Hunter Testimony) (“The attributes that made the M-16 a beneficial
service rifle are also present in the AR-15 rifles.”).  In fact,
with the exception of fully automatic or burst firing mode,
AR-15s are “identical copies of military firearms” that
“retain a number of features originally designed to maximize their effectiveness in combat.”  Report of James E.
Yurgealitis, Viramontes v. Cook County , No. 1:21-cv-
04595 (N.D. Ill. Mar. 3, 2023), Dkt. No. 81-5, at 21
(Yurgealitis Viramontes Report).
A. The Banned AR-15 Shares the Same Design and
Features Intended to Maximize Combat Effectiveness in Service Rifles
The table below, prepared using information from the
Yurgealitis Viramontes Report, demonstrates how AR-
15s are “identical copies of military firearms.”  Yurgealitis
Viramontes Report at 21.

12
This Court has described the AR-15 as “the civilian
version of the military’s M-16 rifle.”  Staples v. United
States, 511 U.S. 600, 603 (1994).  That description reflects
the rifle’s design history.  The AR-15 is a military rifle sold
to civilians with its automatic fire control removed.  Production of the ArmaLite design, developed for the U.S.
military in the early 1960s, was licensed to Colt, and “initially the model designation was, as produced, AR-15.”
Yurgealitis Viramontes Report at 14.  Only later, after a
series of engineering changes, was the military designation “changed to M-16.”  Ibid.  The M16 is thus the AR-15
renamed, not a separate weapon from which the civilian
rifle was copied.  Colt then marketed the semiautomatic
version itself, which differed from the military rifle only
by “removal of fully automatic capability” through a handful of modifications to the fire control system—changes
that “did not change the general overall appearance,
physical features or semi-automatic rate of fire of the rifle.”  Id. at 17–18.
That shared origin persists in the rifles sold today.  As
Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III has observed, “the civilian
versions of the AR-15 have not strayed far from the rifle’s
military origin.”  Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 454.  The “overall
design configuration” of AR-type civilian rifles is “identical or nearly so” to that original production design.
Yurgealitis Viramontes Report at 15.  “[T]he basic configuration, appearance, construction and operation of the internal gas operating system” of the military M16 and civilian AR-15 “[have] remained unchanged since [their] initial inception as a military weapon.”  Id. at 14.  Colonel
Tucker likewise explained that the M16 “is a lightweight,
5.56mm, air-cooled, gas-operated, magazine-fed assault
rifle, with a rotating bolt.  So is the AR-15.  It has the exact
same design.”  Tucker Barnett Report ¶ 15.

13
Amici highlight below the specific similarities between
AR-15 rifles and military rifles and how these similarities
make these weapons most suitable for combat.
Size of Ammunition Rounds : The civilian AR-15 and
military rifles are built to carry the same size rounds:
5.56mm/.223 caliber cartridges.  Yurgealitis  Viramontes
Report at 15; see also Rupp, 723 F. Supp. 3d at 852. These
rounds are “substantially smaller than [those] used in previous service rifles,” giving these weapons “three main advantages” in military combat.  Hunter Testimonyat 5; see
also Yurgealitis Viramontes Report at 15–16 (discussing
how these characteristics “influenced the US Military’s
decision to switch over from the 7.62 x 51mm / .308 caliber
round used in the preceding model M-14 rifles.”).  First,
the smaller size allows troops in combat to carry more
rounds.  Hunter Testimony at 5 (“For the same weight,
four times as many M-16 rounds than M-1 rounds can be
carried.”).  Second, the small size allows troops to fire
more rounds without stopping.  Ibid.  Third, it allows each
round to cause “more damage to the human body.”  Ibid.
Magazine Capacity: The standard magazine for both
the military M16 and the civilian AR-15 holds 30 rounds,
and both platforms accept magazines holding up to 100
rounds.  See  Bianchi , 111 F.4th at 455; Yurgealitis  Viramontes Report at 27.  That shared figure is a military
specification rather than a sporting one.  Semiautomatic
rifles “designed, manufactured and marketed as ‘hunting
rifles’ traditionally have an internal magazine capacity of
less than 10 rounds.”  Yurgealitis  Viramontes Report at
26.  Indeed, large-capacity detachable magazines were not
“initially designed or intended for the civilian marketplace”––rather, they “can be traced directly to a military
heritage.”  Id. at 26–27.  A detachable magazine allows a
combat rifleman to efficiently carry a combat load, to rapidly change magazines in combat, and to significantly reduce reload time.  See Tucker Rupp Report ¶ 15 (“During

14
intense combat, the detachable magazine provides a rifleman the capability to fire 120 rounds on semiautomatic in
three minutes at a high-sustained rate of 45 rounds per
minute.”); see also Rupp, 723 F. Supp. 3d at 854 (“A rifle’s
capability of accepting detachable magazines allows a
shooter to rapidly change magazines and continue firing.
* * * [A] detachable magazine decreases a shooter’s reload time by about 3–5 seconds compared to a fixed magazine.”) (internal citations omitted).  The “ability to fire an
increased quantity of cartridges without reloading increases the lethality and effectiveness of small arms in
combat[,] or the military would not have incorporated this
feature.”  Yurgealitis  Viramontes Report at 27.  In both
civilian AR-15 rifles and military service rifles, “[a]ny increase to magazine capacity increases the killing efficiency.” Tucker Rupp Report ¶ 21 (explaining that this
also applies to large-capacity fixed magazines).
Internal Components: AR-15s contain the same builtin features that make military rifles combat-appropriate.
Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 455.  These features include “a
threaded barrel for the affixing of a flash suppressor, recoil compensator, or silencer,” and a “rail integration system.”  Ibid.  These features make these weapons “combatfunctional.”  Ibid.  Threaded barrels allow the firearm’s
operator to affix features such as flash suppressors and
muzzle compensators, which are themselves combat-functional for reasons explained below.  See ibid.
Weight and Dimensions: Both AR-15 rifles and service
rifles are lightweight and shorter than other rifles, or can
be shortened through commonly added accessories.  Compare Hunter Testimony at 4 (listing the M16’s lighter
weight and shorter length, compared to its military predecessors, as two of its “benefits”) with Report of Dr.
Martin A. Schreiber ¶ 28, Barnett v. Raoul, No. 3:23-cv-
00209 (S.D. Ill. May 31, 2024), Dkt. No. 194-1 (Schreiber
Barnett Report) (describing how AR-15s “tend to be

15
lightweight and highly maneuverable”).  These characteristics are desirable for combat because they “maximize
the accuracy and hence lethality of the individual
shooter,” and allow the weapons to be “easily carried” and
“rapidly and accurately sighted and fired at a target.”
Schreiber Barnett Report ¶ 28.
Combat Accessories: Finally, AR-15s also incorporate
or accept as an accessory many of the same attachable
“combat-functional features” as their military counterparts.  See  Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 455.  These accessories
generally increase the “effectiveness and lethality” of the
weapons, and thus move AR-15s’ functionality “towards
the military side of the spectrum and away from the sporting side.”  Yurgealitis  Viramontes Report at 21–22; see
also Tucker Rupp Report ¶ 22 (explaining that such features “enhance the lethality of both semiautomatic and
automatic rifles and are most appropriate for combat applications when used in conjunction with those types of
weapons systems.”).  Such features include:
 Barrel shrouds: A barrel shroud, or handguard, is a
“combat-functional feature that the AR-15 and M16
share.”  Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 455.  Military rifles have
featured a shroud that encircles the barrel since before World War II.  Yurgealitis Viramontes Report at
23.  This feature protects military operators from injury due to a hot barrel or other component, and provides additional grip space for soldiers to steady the
rifle.  Ibid.  That protection answers a need particular
to combat.  The sustained, rapid fire of combat heats
the barrel quickly in a way that the intermittent shots
of hunting do not, and the shroud is what allows a soldier to keep a firm grip and continue firing “without
being burned.”  Ibid.; see 2016 Manual at 2-13 (describing the challenge of cooling “[l]ightweight weapons like the M4 and M16”).

16
 Pistol grips: The pistol grip (or “rear grip”) beneath a
rifle’s action has functional significance to the military.
Both contemporary AR-15-style rifles and M16s have
incorporated pistol grips that enable fast reloading
and accuracy during sustained firing.  See Bianchi, 111
F.4th at 455.  The pistol grip on a rifle “serves only two
purposes.”  Tucker Rupp Report ¶ 16.  It allows a rifleman to pull the rifle into his shoulder with each shot,
increasing stock weld (required for effective semiautomatic and automatic rapid fire), reducing both semiautomatic and automatic recoil, and reducing barrel rise.
Ibid.  And it “functions as a hand rest to reduce
hand/finger fatigue during long combat engagements.”  Ibid.  These actions “increase the killing efficiency of automatic rifles and are necessities in sustained combat operations of weeks or months when firing a rifle rapidly.”  Ibid.  “Rifles traditionally considered sporting firearms are generally not designed and
produced as such.”  Yurgealitis Viramontes Report at
22.
 Forward grips: The forward grip provides stability
and control of the rifle’s movement during firing.
Tucker Rupp Report ¶ 17.  This can contribute to more
accurate semiautomatic fire.  Id. ¶¶ 14, 16–17.  It allows increased stability of the firearm by the operator,
and allows the operator to better control recoil and
muzzle climb, thus increasing the hit probability of
successive shots.  Yurgealitis  Viramontes Report at
22.  A forward pistol grip can also “help insulate the
non-trigger hand from heat during rapid fire.”  Rupp,
723 F. Supp. 3d at 854.  Forward pistol grips were
added to military rifles to “increase [] killing efficiency.”  Tucker Rupp Report ¶ 17.  They are not features found on traditional sporting firearms; it was not
until the U.S. military adopted Rail Attachment

17
Systems that foregrips for semiautomatic rifles grew
in popularity.  Yurgealitis Viramontes Report at 22.
 Compact stock configurations: The AR-15 rifles, like
many military service rifles, are compatible with compact stock configurations, such as folding or telescoping stocks, which allow a person to drastically reduce
the length of a rifle.  Tucker Rupp Report ¶ 18.  These
configurations respond to specific military needs.
Colonel Tucker explains that a folding stock––which
“causes weapon instability”––was “designed for military personnel” as “weapon[s] for offensive combat”
for soldiers escaping damaged vehicles or abandoning
a destroyed weapon system.  Ibid.  Folding and telescoping stocks also allow the operator to more easily
conceal or maneuver a rifle in a confined space, and
facilitate easier or more comfortable firing from positions other than the shoulder.  Yurgealitis Viramontes
Report at 23; see also  Rupp, 723 F. Supp. 3d at 854
(“[A] telescoping stock ‘renders [a] rifle more concealable.’”) (internal citation omitted).
 Flash suppressors: Another “combat-functional” design feature that appears in both the civilian AR-15 rifles and service rifles is the flash suppressor.  Bianchi,
111 F.4th at 455.  A flash suppressor both “conceals a
shooter’s position and facilitates night combat operations.”  Ibid.  As Colonel Tucker explains, the “purpose
of the flash suppressor is to reduce combat signature
by cooling and dispersing burning gases,” which
“makes it more difficult for the enemy to pinpoint a rifleman’s location” and “facilitates night combat operations by reducing muzzle flash and mitigating muzzle
flash impact on night vision goggles.”  Tucker  Rupp
Report ¶ 20.  For these reasons, this “accessory serves
specific combat-oriented purposes.”  Ibid.
 Muzzle brakes/recoil compensators: In addition to pistol grips and forward grips, muzzle brakes and recoil

18
compensators are devices attached to or built into the
end of a firearm barrel to diminish the recoil of the
firearm, making it easier to fire a gun rapidly.  Bianchi,
111 F.4th at 455 (characterizing a recoil compensator,
which can be affixed to the threaded barrel of an AR-
15/M16, as a “combat functional feature”).  A muzzle
brake in a civilian semiautomatic rifle can serve a number of purposes depending on its design and placement, such as allowing the operator to regain control
of the rifle more rapidly after firing.  Yurgealitis  Viramontes Report at 23.  The “net advantage” of the
operator’s faster recovery of control of the rifle after
firing “is that it allows the operator to more rapidly
reacquire targets [and] fire accurate additional shots
if required.”  Id. at 24.
B. AR-15 Rifles and Service Rifles Have the Same
Capacity to Inflict Severe Injury
The AR-15 rifle is just as destructive and lethal as service rifles like the M4 and M16.  All are “designed for the
purpose of maximum killing in wartime settings.”
Schreiber Barnett Report ¶ 44.  “When operated in semiauto mode, the AR-15 and M4 share the same rates of fire,
the same maximum effective range, the same maximum
range, use the same magazines designed for combat and
the same ammunition.”  Tucker  Rupp  Report ¶ 13.  In
short, “AR-15s and the like are designed to empower an
individual soldier to kill as many people in as little time as
possible.”  Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 465; see also Barnett, 180
F.4th at 1054 (“AR-15s, in other words, are dangerous not
only in the sense that all firearms are dangerous but also
relative to the semiautomatic handguns that Heller confirmed are protected.”).
AR-15s are “deadly accurate weapons with enormous
destructive capacity.”  Schreiber  Barnett  Report ¶ 44.
The AR-15 has an effective range of 400–500 yards,

19
making it “highly accurate at great distances.”  Id. ¶ 29.
Additionally, the AR-15 has a muzzle velocity of approximately 3,200 feet per second and kinetic energy of 1,303
foot-pounds.  Id. ¶¶ 21−22.  This results in phenomenal
force that can inflict significant damage.  See, e.g., Hunter
Testimony at 5 (the speed of assault rifle bullets “contributes to the amount of damage that rounds fired are able
to inflict.”); Yurgealitis Viramontes Report at 30 (assault
weapons risk “overpenetration of common household materials.”); id. at 31 (noting that commonly available
5.56mm/.223 caliber ammunition can penetrate Level III
body armor); Capen, 708 F. Supp. 3d at 86 (“Rounds from
an AR-15 can pass through most construction materials,
even at ranges of 350 yards.”).
The AR-15’s “round is designed to kill, not wound.”
Tucker Rupp  Report ¶ 13.  Dr. Martin Schreiber has
treated hundreds of patients suffering from gunshot
wounds, both as a civilian surgeon and on military deployments.  He found that AR-15 wounds he treated in civilians “were identical to the wounds made by the M16s” in
combat.  Schreiber Barnett Report ¶¶ 34–36.
The severity and complexity of wounds from AR-15s
increase the chances of complications and fatality.  Id.
¶¶ 36–39.  When a bullet from a firearm penetrates the
human body, it creates a cavity.  The “larger the cavity,
the more severe the injury.”  Id. ¶ 23.  The kinetic energy
and force generated by the AR-15 “mean[] that a round
fired by such a weapon typically creates a relatively large
temporary cavity in a human body, with devastating effects to tissue and surrounding organs.”  Id. ¶ 24.  Further, the lightweight bullets used in these weapons “are
disrupted when they hit flesh, and shatter bone, resulting
in an erratic pattern that causes extensive damage.”
Hunter Testimony at 5; see also Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 455
(“The ‘catastrophic’ damage caused by AR-15 rounds
means that the injuries they leave in their wake––such as

20
‘multiple organs shattered,’ bones ‘exploded,’ and ‘soft tissue absolutely destroyed’––‘often cannot be repaired’ by
trauma surgeons.”) (internal citations omitted).
The accuracy, efficiency, and reliability of AR-15s,
combined with their semiautomatic rate of fire, also contribute to their lethality.  These qualities enable a shooter
to “deliver the large kinetic energy” generated by the firearm repeatedly, “either to the same victim or to multiple
victims.”  Schreiber Barnett Report ¶ 25.  A “higher rate
of fire creates greater potential lethality, but bullets have
to hit their target to be lethal”––and AR-15s “are also designed to maximize the accuracy and hence lethality of the
individual shooter.”  Id. ¶¶ 27–28.  Due to their low recoil,
shooters can also continue firing without having to resight, or re-aim, the weapon at the target: “the shooter is
able to keep the assault weapon still and produce a consistently straight line of fire.”  Id. ¶ 28.  This can “increase
the number of victims and lethality of injuries per event.”
Id. ¶ 25; see also Rupp, 723 F. Supp. 3d at 853 (noting that
the combination of an AR-15’s lethality and rapid-fire capability “allow[s] ‘a shooter to kill dozens of people within
a matter of seconds.’”) (internal citations omitted).
Together, the “high kinetic energy, the ability to fire
rounds rapidly, deadly accuracy at a great distance, a high
degree of maneuverability, low recoil, and the instability
of the projectile––coupled with enhancements to accuracy
for an individual shooter––results in maximum killing potential” that is appropriate only on the battlefield.
Schreiber Barnett Report ¶ 30.  Put simply, an AR-15 rifle
is an “offensive combat weapon no different in function or
purpose” than service rifles––with both weapons “designed to kill as many people as possible, as efficiently as
possible.”  Tucker  Rupp Report ¶ 22; see also Dempsey
Barnett Report ¶ 21(a) (describing the purpose of military
service rifles as “placing well-aimed fire on the enemy.”).

21
CONCLUSION
For these reasons, and those set forth by respondents,
the judgments below should be affirmed.
